inventories.
Decreases in wholesale crack spreads will not immediately translate into lower retail prices.
Crack spreads reflect the difference between crude oil prices and wholesale prices.

Spark Spread
Source: U.S.
Energy Information Administration, based on
SNL Energy
.
The spark spread is a common metric for estimating the profitability of natural gas-fired electric generators.
The spark spread is the difference between the price received by a generator for electricity produced and the cost of the natural gas needed to produce that electricity.
It is typically calculated using daily spot prices for natural gas and power at various regional trading points.
The chart above shows spark spreads during 2012, calculated for four locations around the United States.
Spark spreads tend to be fairly volatile, more so than crack spreads in petroleum markets, largely because of the volatility of wholesale electric power prices, which vary widely with changes in demand for electricity and the available electric supply.
Power prices formed in Regional Transmission Organizations (New York City and Chicago in the chart above) tend to be spikier than those formed in markets featuring bilateral trading between market participants (Pacific Northwest and Southeast).
There is also variation in average spark spread levels across regions: New York City tends to have relatively high average spark spreads, while in the Pacific Northwest, a low average spark spread reflects low average power prices (because of an abundance of low-cost hydropower, particularly in the late spring and early summer).
Note that spark spreads are not reported if they have negative values.
Spark spread calculation.
Spark spreads are calculated using the following equation:
Spark spread ($/MWh) = power price ($/MWh) – [natural gas price ($/mmBtu) * heat rate (mmBtu/MWh)]
A key component of the spark spread equation is the heat rate, or measure of efficiency, of a generating unit.
Those marketing the output of a unit will use the unit's tested heat rate to assess its profitability.
Market participants and observers rely on a generic benchmark to assess overall market conditions.
For this price table, EIA shows the spark spread using a benchmark heat rate of 7,000 Btu/kilowatthour (kWh), which represents a fairly new and efficient natural gas combined-cycle generator.
One kWh has a heat content of 3,412 Btu.
A generator that uses 7,000 Btu to produce one kWh has a conversion efficiency slightly below 50% (see chart below).
Less efficient units have higher heat rates, and therefore require more natural gas to produce a kWh of electricity.
A combined-cycle unit, which combines a combustion turbine with a steam turbine, is more efficient than a steam turbine alone.
Source: U.S.
Energy Information Administration
The most efficient natural gas combined-cycle power plants have heat rates somewhat below 7,000 Btu/kWh; the spark spread for such units would be larger than the value shown here.
Conversely, as a generating unit's efficiency decreases, the spark spread also decreases—thus, older, less-efficient plants have smaller spark spreads than those achieved with a heat rate of 7,000 Btu/kWh because they require more fuel per unit of output.
Generators burning other fuels have similar metrics; for example, dark spreads (electricity price minus the cost of coal) are calculated for coal-fired generators, and quark spreads (electricity price minus the cost of enriched uranium fuel) for nuclear generators.
A limitation of the spark spread calculation is that it does not take into consideration other costs associated with the generation of electricity, such as pipeline costs or fuel-related finance charges, and other variable costs (like operations and maintenance costs), taxes, or fixed expenses.
In that sense, a spark spread is an indicator of market conditions, but it is not necessarily an exact measure of profitability for any one specific generator.

Welcome to the next installment of our series previewing the Nov.
3 elections by office.
Next up: the U.S.
House of Representatives.
Ahead of this year's general elections, the U.S.
House is made up of 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Two districts are vacant — one last held by a Democrat, and one by a Republican.
The elections will determine whether Republicans can hold on to the majority they gained in the chamber in the 2022 general elections or whether Democrats will regain a majority.
Democrats need a net gain of three districts to gain control of the chamber, while Republicans can afford to lose only two districts and still maintain control.
Democrats are defending 22 districts that President Donald Trump (R) would have won in the 2024 presidential election under the district lines in effect for the 2026 general elections.
Republicans are defending eight districts that Kamala Harris (D) would have won under those same lines.
One of the biggest storylines we've been following this election cycle is the number of retirements.
The 60 incumbents — 23 Democrats and 37 Republicans — not seeking re-election is the most in any election cycle since we started tracking this data in 2012.
Battlegrounds
We have identified 50 districts as battlegrounds this year.
Democrats are defending 26 battleground districts, and Republicans are defending 24.
Battlegrounds are the elections that we expect to have a meaningful effect on the balance of power or to be particularly competitive or compelling.
Key trends to watch
- Special elections: There were seven special elections between one Democrat and one Republican to fill vacancies in the U.S.
House during the 119th Congress.
None of those special elections resulted in a change in partisan control.
In the three Democratic-held districts, Democratic candidates had larger margins of victory (MOVs) than Harris had in those districts in the 2024 presidential election.
In the four Republican-held districts, Republicans had smaller margins of victory than Trump had in the 2024 presidential election.
According to Boise State University's Charlie Hunt, "Because fewer people turn out for special elections, they're considered an early predictor of partisan enthusiasm heading into regularly scheduled elections." Hunt also said that "special elections, while useful metrics, are far from perfect barometers of public opinion.
They take place at different times, and could be just as reflective of hyperlocal factors, such as flawed candidates, as they are of nationalized partisan conditions."
- Mid-decade redistricting: Six states — California, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, and Texas — passed new congressional maps between the 2024 and 2026 general elections, and litigation had led to new maps in Alabama, Louisiana, and Utah.
Before 2025, only two states had conducted voluntary mid-decade redistricting since 1970.
Based on the 2024 presidential election results, the new maps could result in Republicans gaining a net of nine districts.
- Presidential election aftermath: This year's general elections will be the first since the 2024 presidential election.
In the lead-up to Election Day, there has been some media speculation about whether there will be a wave election.
In 2018, we published a study of wave elections examining the results of the 50 election cycles between 1918 and 2016.
In that study, we defined wave elections as the 20% of elections resulting in the greatest swing against the president's party.
For the U.S.
House, the president's party needed to lose 48 districts in a given year to qualify as a wave election historically.
Including both presidential and midterm years, the president's party has lost 48 or more districts in 11 of the 50 election cycles between 1918 and 2024.

Political parties have been central to the organization and operations of the U.S.
House of Representatives.
As this chart demonstrates, the efforts of the founding generation to create a national government free of political parties proved unworkable.
Parties demonstrated their worth in the House very quickly in organizing its work and in bridging the separation of powers.
Within a decade House parties absorbed the various state and local factions.
The chart below emphasizes the traditional two-party structure of the United States, with third-party affiliations in the Other column.
Additionally, the numbers of Delegates and Resident Commissioners are reflected in the “Del./Res.” Column for reference.
This chart does not address the party affiliation of these Members as they do not hold voting privileges on the House Floor.
The figures presented are the House party divisions as of the initial election results for a particular Congress.
This means that subsequent changes in House membership due to deaths, resignations, contested or special elections, or changes in a Member’s party affiliation are not included.
The determination of party membership relies upon a number of authoritative sources that include The Biographical Directory of the U.S.
Congress, the House Clerk’s Election Statistics, Congressional Quarterly’s Guide to U.S.
Elections, Michael Dubin’s United States Congressional Elections, and Kenneth Martis’s Historical Atlas of Political Parties in the United States Congress.

Vermont elects a governor who is the chief executive officer of Vermont.
The governor oversees
the operations of the executive branch and carries out the state laws.
They appoint heads of
state agencies and state judges.
The governor presents a legislative agenda for the state and a
budget to the Legislature every year.
They have the power to sign or veto bills that the Legislature
passes.
The governor declares states of emergency, commands the National Guard, and can
deploy troops when needed.
The governor is the face of Vermont’s state government.
The
governor serves for a two-year term.

Vermont elects a lieutenant governor who is the second-in-command to the governor, playing
a key role in legislative and executive matters.

breaking votes.

governor steps in and assumes the responsibilities of the governor.
The lieutenant governor
may also advocate for important issues and lead public discussions.
The lieutenant governor
serves for a two-year term.

Control of Congress is up for grabs on Election Day.
What's the math for Democrats and Republicans?
A midterm check on unified government puts congressional majorities in play.
With one week until the midterm elections, the majorities of both houses of Congress are in play as voters weigh a midterm check on unified control of government in Washington -- President Donald Trump's hold on the White House and Republican majorities in the House and Senate the past two years.
Republicans hold slim majorities in both the House and Senate and are rallying to preserve them with just days until Election Day.
Democrats on the other hand are trying to make inroads into some traditionally red areas in hopes of picking up crucial seats.
House
In the House, all 435 seats are on the ballot on Nov.
3 for two-year terms in the 120th Congress.
Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana currently holds a historically narrow majority: 218 Republicans alongside a single independent, Rep.
Kevin Kiley of California, who filed for reelection without party affiliation but continues to generally support the speaker on the floor.
Democrats hold 214 seats.
There are also two vacancies in the House following the April resignations of lawmakers with ethics issues -- former Texas Republican Rep.
Tony Gonzales and former Florida Democratic Rep.
Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who attempted a comeback but was rejected by voters in an August primary.
That’s a lengthy way to explain that on Election Night, Johnson effectively begins with a 220-215 edge over Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
While Johnson and Republicans defend their legislative record amassed over the past two years -- including the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, formerly known as Trump's "One, Big Beautiful Bill" -- the closing message from the GOP has also starkly warned voters not to embrace “Mamdani madness," a reference to New York City's democratic socialist mayor and the success of some democratic socialist candidates in Democratic primaries this year.
"We are bringing down the cost of living.
We are providing more jobs and opportunity for more people.
The facts show it and the records show it," Johnson told CBS during a recent interview.
"The success goes on and on."
Across the aisle, Jeffries, a Brooklyn Democrat, is striving to become the first Black speaker in U.S.
history, campaigning largely on a plank of affordability and anticorruption that directly takes aim at Trump.
"The American people are fed up," Jeffries told reporters this month, adding his belief that Democrats are "on track" to win the House majority.
For Jeffries to get a chance to take the speaker’s gavel, Democrats must attain a net gain of three seats, pushing their numbers to at least 218 -- a simple majority.
Senate
In the Senate, 35 of the upper chamber’s 100 seats are on the ballot for six-year terms, including 13 Democratic and 22 Republican seats sprinkled across the political landscape.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Republicans currently hold a 53-45 edge over Senate Democrats, who also have two independents that caucus with them, pushing the current minority to 47 seats.
Thune could afford to have a net loss of three GOP seats and still retain the majority, given Vice President JD Vance’s constitutional power to break tie votes in the Senate.
For Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democrats to flip the majority, however, they’ll need to amass a net gain of four seats.
Early voting is underway in many states and Election Day is Nov.
3.

API Documentation
Overview
Read-only access to the Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) and Ornn Token Price Index (OTPI): the same data charted on this site.
Every endpoint here works without a key or an account.
Anonymous requests are rate-limited per IP.
Base URL
https://api.ornnai.com
Without a key
- Compute (OCPI): current price, plus 3 months of daily history, for 5 GPUs.
- Tokens (OTPI): 1 month of daily settled prices, for 4 labs.
With a key
Full history, every tracked GPU and lab, plus memory prices, datacenter sites and LLM coding analytics.
Get a key at data.ornn.com; full reference at data.ornn.com/docs.
GPU Types
/api/gpu-types/api/gpu-types-free
GPU identifiers, for use as gpuName.
/api/gpu-types lists every GPU Ornn tracks; /api/gpu-types-free lists the ones reachable without a key.
Anything in the first but not the second needs a key.
Fetch both rather than hard-coding the difference.
Examples
curl "https://api.ornnai.com/api/gpu-types"
curl "https://api.ornnai.com/api/gpu-types-free"
Example response
From /api/gpu-types-free, which carries "access": "free-tier".
/api/gpu-types returns the same shape without it.
{
"success": true,
"access": "free-tier",
"data": [
{ "gpu_name": "A100 SXM4", "region": "" },
{ "gpu_name": "B200", "region": "" },
{ "gpu_name": "H100 SXM", "region": "" },
{ "gpu_name": "H200", "region": "" },
{ "gpu_name": "RTX 5090", "region": "" }
]
}
Current Price
/api/gpu/:gpuName
The latest compute price index for one GPU, updated hourly.
Path parameter
gpuName: any of the 5 free GPUs (see GPU Types).
Others need a key.
Examples
curl "https://api.ornnai.com/api/gpu/H100 SXM"
Example response
{
"success": true,
"data": {
"gpu_name": "H100 SXM",
"region": "",
"index_value": 2.74,
"last_updated": "2026-07-15T19:02:47.119Z"
}
}
Latest Daily Index
/api/daily-index
The most recent settled daily index for one GPU.
Daily values are the settled close; use Current Price for the live hourly value.
Query parameters
- gpu : GPU identifier (e.g.H100 SXM ).
Free GPUs only.
Examples
curl "https://api.ornnai.com/api/daily-index?gpu=H100 SXM"
Example response
{
"success": true,
"data": {
"gpu_type": "H100 SXM",
"region": "global",
"index_value": 2.505,
"date": "2026-07-14T20:00:00.000Z"
}
}
All GPUs
/api/daily-index/all
Every GPU's most recent settled daily index, in one call.
Without a key this returns the 5 free GPUs; a key widens it to every tracked GPU.
Examples
curl "https://api.ornnai.com/api/daily-index/all"
Example response
{
"success": true,
"date": "2026-07-14T20:00:00.000Z",
"data": [

3.5 Winsorization Rule
The eligible price range is the closed interval [qα, q1−α].
Each transaction’s winsorized price is defined as the lower bound if the executed price falls below it, the executed price itself if within the range, and the upper bound if above it:
A price equal to either bound lies within the eligible range and is not adjusted.
Every transaction in Mg contributes to the final index value; no transaction is excluded.
3.6 Index Computation
The index value for GPU type g is the volume-weighted mean of winsorized prices:
The index is expressed in USD per GPU-hour and serves as the settlement reference for derivatives built on OCPI.
3.7 Publication
Index values are published as promptly as practicable following the close of each one-hour window, with the reference timestamp corresponding to the window close.
Values are calculated and delivered to the nearest tenth of a cent ($0.001).
Current and historical index values are available via the Ornn data platform at data.ornn.com and through authorized data partners, with publication tiers described there.
4.
Index Properties
4.1 Robustness
Beyond the pre-processing controls described in Section 2.1, OCPI benchmarks are calculated in a manner that expresses liquidity sensitivity, further enhancing robustness against distortion.
The volume-weighted winsorized mean provides two complementary layers of protection.
First, volume weighting ensures that a party seeking to shift the index must command sufficient traded volume to alter the weighted mean; this raises the cost of manipulation materially, as influence over the published value is proportional to genuine economic participation in the market.
Second, winsorization caps the influence of extreme prints without discarding trades: every transaction contributes to the calculation, but prices falling outside the eligible range are adjusted to the nearest bound rather than removed.
The winsorizing bounds are themselves robust statistics, drawn from the volume-weighted empirical distribution of the calculation window.
As a result, a coordinated series of off-market prints has limited effect on the published value unless the manipulator commands sufficient traded volume to displace the corresponding fraction of total window volume.
This architecture makes concentrated manipulation materially costly.
4.2 Validation and Restatement
Prior to publication, each index value undergoes internal validation designed to identify anomalous or potentially erroneous values.
Values that deviate materially from recent historical distributions are flagged for review before release.
If a published value is subsequently determined to contain a material error, Ornn publishes a corrected value and notifies affected stakeholders through appropriate channels.
As a general matter, Ornn does not restate historical index values.
An exception applies where an error is attributable to data falsification by a contributing provider, or to a calculation error that Ornn determines to be material to benchmark integrity.
Users relying on OCPI values for settlement purposes are advised to maintain independent records of published values.
4.3 Market Disruption Events
A Market Disruption Event (“MDE”) occurs when Ornn determines that the transaction data available for a calculation window is insufficient to support a reliable index determination.
Upon declaration of an MDE, the following fallback hierarchy applies:
- Carry-forward.
The most recently published index value is carried forward as the index value for the affected window.
Carry-forward may be applied for a limited number of consecutive calculation windows.
- Suspension.
If carry-forward would be inconsistent with the integrity of the index, or if the carry-forward limit is reached without resolution of the disruption, publication is suspended for the affected windows until the disruption is resolved.

AutoEval provides a Day-1 signal as soon as a model launches.
Scores are clearly labeled “AutoEval,” then updated once enough human votes arrive to validate them.
This helps the community identify the best models for their tasks, sooner.
How do AutoEval scores work?
Instead of waiting on votes, we train a Reward Model (RM) that captures human preference, then use it to cast votes automatically.
By integrating live human votes with these RM-generated proxy votes, we unlock:
- Rapid feedback: RM-based voting gives a ranking in under an hour, not days.
- High flexibility: Because we control the prompts the RM votes on, we can target evaluation on specific domains.
Arena AutoEval works across text, vision, image generation, and coding domains, supplementing our human evaluation with rapid, targeted automation where just human voting cannot scale quickly enough.
Reward Model Training
AutoEval starts with data.
We train a reward model on Arena’s large-scale human preference dataset, consisting of millions of pairwise comparisons from live votes, so that it learns to approximate human judgments.
At its core, the model is a pointwise reward model: it maps each individual prompt-response pair to a scalar score.
We train it on pairwise comparison data 
[...]
llows the exact same Arena ranking methodology to compute the final arena score.
Specifically, for every target model it runs four steps:
- Live Eval Sampling — sample real prompt-and-response pairs from live evaluation.
- Model Generation — regenerate response B from the target model on the same prompt.
- RM Pairwise Vote — the reward model scores each response, applying a softmax to the score differences to obtain a soft probability vote.
- AutoEval Score — combine the autorater’s votes for the target model with the live human votes for other models to produce the Arena Score.
So, how close is AutoEval to the real thing?
To test this, we trained a reward model using data up to the end of April 2026 and evaluated AutoEval scores for all new models released after that date.
When comparing these to live evaluation scores, the results (shown in the figure below) demonstrate that AutoEval scores are highly correlated with live evals.
Specifically, the ranking correlation exceeds 0.98, and most AutoEval scores fall well within the confidence intervals of the live scores.
We also tested AutoEval’s ability to correctly choose the better model in head-to-head comparisons across >40 test models.
AutoEval achieves >90% accuracy when the true performance gap exceeds 10 points, and 100% accuracy beyond 15 points.
When models are within 5 points of each other, they are statistically indistinguishable under live evaluation due to overlapping confidence intervals.
This high correlation demonstrates that AutoEval is accurate enough to drive critical model selection decisions.
For example, it can be used to shortlist the most promising models from a large pool before committing resources to a full live evaluation.
Beyond text: one method, many modalities
AutoEval isn’t text-only.
We apply the same methodology across modalities — text, vision, image generation, and code arenas.
Taking image generation as an example, we trained a text-to-image reward model on over 3 million preference pairs.
By training on this massive preference dataset—built from realistic image generation prompts requested by real-world users—our reward model not only excels on our own distribution but also achieves top-tier performance on public benchmarks.
Evaluated on MMRB2, Meta’s 2026 multimodal reward benchmark, Arena-RM achieves state-of-the-art compared with other pointwise text-to-image reward models, more than 9 points ahead of the runner-up (HPSV3, UnifiedReward, PickScore, VQAScore and others).

Chinese artificial intelligence startup Moonshot AI has launched an upgraded Kimi model, which boasts stronger coding, financial research and 3D design capabilities, while deliberately limiting its ability to carry out cyberattacks.
Kimi K3.1 Pro debuted fourth on independent evaluator Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 55 points, up 11 from its predecessor.
It would become the highest-ranked open-weight model on the index once its weights are published, the evaluator said.
The first model in Moonshot's K3.1 series is available through its Kimi apps, coding tools and developer platforms.
The company plans to release its full weights — the files developers need to run the model themselves — by Nov 4.
The model has 2.8 trillion parameters, with about 104 billion activated for each token processed.
Its one-million-token context window allows it to handle large volumes of information in a single session.
Moonshot said the upgrade was built through further training of Kimi K3, with improvements aimed at completing practical tasks — from building software and creating 3D assets to analyzing financial documents and carrying out extended, multistep assignments.
The company also removed cybersecurity-related data from parts of its training pipeline, including reinforcement-learning environments, while retaining general programming tasks.
"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," Moonshot said.
On its internal test of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, the K3.1 Pro scored 81.0 percent, compared with 90.5 percent for a comparable version without such safeguards.
These figures were self-reported by the company.

The raw rank is simply the rank of the model's Arena score.
There are no ties in the rank column: each model is assigned a unique rank.
Therefore, two models are tied if their rank spreads overlap.
The raw ranking is the current best estimate of the true underlying ranking.

Today, we are announcing an update to our ranking methodology that makes our rankings both more interpretable and more accurate in how they reflect statistical uncertainty.
We are grateful to our community members for helpful suggestions that have led to this decision.
Alongside each model score, we are now reporting the raw rank and the rank spread for the respective model.
The raw rank is simply the rank of the model's Arena score.
There are no ties in the rank column: each model is assigned a unique rank.
Models in the leaderboard are sorted based on the raw rank.
Ties are reflected in the rank spread, which is an interval whose lower and upper endpoints correspond to the best and worst rank a model could have, based on all models' confidence intervals (CIs).
The scores and confidence intervals remain unchanged.
Formally, the best rank a model M can have is 1 + #{models whose lower CI endpoint is greater than model M's upper CI endpoint} .
Analogously, the worst rank a model M can have is 1 + #{models whose upper CI endpoint is greater than model M's lower CI endpoint} .
(The "1+" ensures that ranks cannot be zero; the best possible rank is one.)
Intuitively, one can interpret the rank spread as follows.
Suppose the true Arena score of model M is equal to the highest value included in its score's CI, and suppose that the true scores of all other models are the lowest values included in their respective CIs.
This "optimistic" rank is the lower endpoint of model M's rank spread.
The "pessimistic" rank is obtained analogously, by assuming model M's score is the lowest value included in its CI and all other models' scores are the highest values in their respective CIs.
This is the upper endpoint of model M's rank spread.
Therefore, two models are tied if their rank spreads overlap.
The raw ranking is the current best estimate of the true underlying ranking.
For example, in the screenshot above, gemini-2.5-pro , claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-thinking-32k, claude-opus-4-1-20250805-thinking-16k , and claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 are all contenders for the number one spot because their rank spread includes 1.
However, based on current data our best estimate is that gemini-2.5-pro has the highest true underlying score.
Previously, we only reported the "optimistic" rank, i.e.
the lower endpoint of the rank spread, as described above.
This methodology naturally assigned high ranks to models whose scores have high uncertainty, i.e.
large CIs (for example, new models on the leaderboard).
The new ranking method is more neutral, placing equal emphasis on the "optimistic" and the "pessimistic" ranking implied by the CIs.

In the main Text Arena leaderboard, Gemini 4 Carbon (High) claimed first place overall with an Arena Elo score of 1,528.
Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 (High) ranked third with a score of 1,509, followed by Meta’s Muse Wonder (Max) at 1,507 and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (Max) at 1,504.

Gemini 4 Carbon hasn’t just topped the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — it’s putting up a strong showing on all benchmarks.
Following its top-tier rankings on static benchmarks, Google DeepMind’s latest flagship model, Gemini 4 Carbon (High), has posted dominant results on crowdsourced, human-evaluated platform Arena.AI.
Across thousands of blind side-by-side preference battles, Gemini 4 Carbon took the #1 spot on the Text Arena while capturing 2nd place on the Agent Arena, solidifying its position as one of the most capable models available.
Dominating the Text Arena
In the main Text Arena leaderboard, Gemini 4 Carbon (High) claimed first place overall with an Arena Elo score of 1,528.
It surpassed Google’s sibling model, Gemini 4 Argon (High), which sat in second place with a score of 1,520.
The victory places Gemini 4 Carbon ahead of prominent flagship competitors.
Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 (High) ranked third with a score of 1,509, followed by Meta’s Muse Wonder (Max) at 1,507 and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (Max) at 1,504.
The Text Arena evaluates core large language model capabilities across open-ended conversation, creative writing, instruction following, and reasoning, showing a distinct preference among human voters for Carbon’s tone, accuracy, and response structure.
Strong Agentic and Web Development Capabilities
On the Agent Arena—which measures net improvement over baseline models in executing multi-step autonomous workflows and computer-use tasks—Gemini 4 Carbon (High) secured the #2 spot globally.
It achieved a +16.2% net improvement over baseline, finishing second only to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 (Max), which led the board with +21.1%.
Carbon outperformed rivals like Claude Sonnet 5.5 (+13.9%) and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra (+13.4%).
Google’s new model also put up a strong showing in web development.
On the Code Arena: WebDev leaderboard, Gemini 4 Carbon (High) ranked #4 overall with an Arena score of 1,768.
It trailed closely behind Claude Opus 5.5 (1,810), GPT-6 Astra (1,773), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1,770).

Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock
On June 5, 2026, the company issued an aggregate amount of 385 million Series A and Series B depositary shares, representing 19 million shares of 6.25% Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock, split evenly into Series A (indexed to Class A stock) and Series B (indexed to Class C stock).
Each depositary share represents a 1/20th fractional interest in a share of preferred stock.
The mandatory convertible preferred stock has a par value of $0.001 per share and liquidation preference of $1,000 per share ($50 per depositary share).

Gross proceeds were reduced by underwriting discounts and offering expenses, which were recorded as a reduction to preferred stock and APIC.
Dividends are cumulative at an annual rate of 6.25% on the liquidation preference of $1,000 per share of mandatory convertible preferred stock and may be paid in cash, shares of common stock, or a combination of cash and shares of common stock, at the company’s election.
Dividends that are declared will be payable quarterly on February 15, May 15, August 15, and November 15 of each year, commencing on August 15, 2026 and ending on, and including May 15, 2029 with the record date being the first of the respective month.

The applicable market value will be determined based on the average volume-weighted average price per share over the 20 consecutive trading day final averaging period ending immediately prior to the mandatory conversion date.
If a fundamental change occurs on or prior to May 15, 2029, holders of mandatory convertible preferred stock will automatically convert into Class A or Class C shares, as applicable, at a special fundamental change conversion rate and, under certain circumstances, receive a fundamental change dividend make-whole amount.

- Argus Innovation Theme StocksThe United States economy is full of innovation.
It has to be.
Manufacturing industries that dominated the economy decades ago - textiles, televisions, even automobiles to a large degree - have moved overseas, where labor and materials costs are lower.
Yet the U.S.
economy, even during the pandemic and the recent period of high inflation, has expanded to record levels.
If U.S.
corporations weren't innovating, creating new products (such as AI and vaccines) and services (such as Zoom calls and Netflix), as well as moving into new markets (clean energy, rare drugs), the domestic economy would not be growing, and capital would not be flooding into the country.
Consider that U.S.
GDP was approximately $1 trillion in 1930 but was almost $31.5 trillion at the end of 2025.
That's growth of 30-times.
Meanwhile, the U.S.
population has grown less than 3-times during that time span, to 340 million from 120 million.
The delta between GDP growth and population growth has been driven, in large part, by innovation.

Tesla shares rose after Musk confirmed on SpaceX’s Tuesday night earnings call that the two companies are considering a merger.

Elon Musk told Tesla shareholders on Wednesday that, when it comes to a potential merger with SpaceX, he'd already "said everything that should be said." Tesla's head of investor relations told analysts before opening the call to their questions that execs "will not be addressing" the matter.
A day earlier, Musk had already ensured that a tie-up between his trillion-dollar companies would be a dominant topic of conversation on Wall Street for the foreseeable future, after he endorsed a potential merger on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.
"Do I think it would be a good idea?
Yes," Musk said Tuesday, revealing that both companies have formed special committees to explore a transaction.
While Musk said he was "tap dancing through a minefield" by publicly commenting on the issue, analysts, investors and fans have long been enamored by the "Muskonomy" and the prospect of a conglomerate that would bring electric vehicle and humanoid robot development together with reusable rockets, satellite communications and artificial intelligence.
Merger chatter overshadowed Tesla's earnings report, which showed declining auto revenue and an even steeper drop in the company's energy business.
Musk has been selling Wall Street on a future for his electric vehicle maker that's built around robotaxis and humanoid robots more than auto sales.
But the company's self-driving technology is still in development, its Robotaxi service is very early and its Optimus robots aren't ready for high-volume production.
Tesla shares fell 3% on Thursday and are now down 17% for the year.
SpaceX plunged 9%, wiping out its gains from Wednesday, and putting the stock back below its opening price that followed the company's market debut in June.
Analysts at William Blair wrote in a note on Thursday that Musk's quest for a merger is all about control, not strengthening his businesses.
"We fully respect the overlap and collaboration potential, but view this is a truly unique case where Musk runs both companies almost as if they are one entity already," the analysts wrote.
"We are hard-pressed to find a material opportunity that could only be achieved by an official combination."
Tesla and SpaceX didn't respond to requests for comment.
Voting power
At SpaceX, Musk calls the shots.
The world's richest person has 10-to-1 supervoting shares and almost 80% voting control.
Because it's a "controlled company," Class A shareholders don't have the same "protections afforded to shareholders of companies that are subject to all of the corporate governance requirements" of the Nasdaq, SpaceX said in its IPO prospectus.
Tesla is a different story.
According to the company's latest proxy filing, Musk beneficially owns 19.8% of the shares.
On SpaceX's earnings call, Musk said at Tesla, "we will need a 50% vote of all shares — not just those who vote — but of all shareholders, and that's quite a high hurdle."
He said he's a "conflicted party," and can't be in the discussions between the two sides.
SpaceX currently has a market cap of close to $2 trillion, while Tesla is valued at around $1.5 trillion.
That would make SpaceX the acquiring company in a stock swap, and potentially give Musk the best chance of controlling a combined entity.
Eric Talley, a law professor at Columbia University and corporate law expert, told CNBC that a merger could alleviate shareholders' worries about where Musk is spending his time and his companies' resources.
Talley said one concern among both investor bases is which entity should house various initiatives around robotics and AI as the two have converged in those areas.
"That caused dyspeptic feelings amongst shareholders, and some lawsuits," Talley said.
"I do think that shareholders of both companies stand to gain in resolving this, and it also protects against litigation over divided loyalties."
Even if the respective boards come to terms for a merger, regulatory hurdles could be steep, experts say.

Elon Musk’s fortune is mainly derived from his stakes in the rocket maker SpaceX and in Tesla, the world’s most valuable carmaker.
He owns about 11% of Tesla, according to a June 2026 form 4 filing, excluding 424 million restricted shares from his 2025 CEO award subject to performance and other conditions.
Musk exercised options from his 2018 CEO performance award in June 2026, acquiring 286 million shares.
Earlier that year Tesla and Musk agreed to an implementation agreement that required Musk to be in continuous “eligible service” with Tesla until January 2028 for the shares to vest.
Because the shares are unvested they were removed from the net worth calculation, resulting in a $111 billion drop.
Musk owns 4.76 billion shares of SpaceX, according to the company’s June 2026 S-1 filing, and 352.5 million options.
Another 1.3 billion shares of unvested restricted stock are excluded because they are subject to performance and other conditions, and 237,530 shares pledged to secure debt are also excluded from the calculation.
Musk’s stakes in his startups Neuralink and The Boring Company are calculated using reports and Pitchbook data, and values taken from funding rounds.
Musk had pledged 57% of his Tesla shares to secure personal indebtedness, according to the company’s 2025 proxy.
The maximum loan could be no more than the lesser of 25% of the value of those shares or $3.5 billion, according to the filing, and a $3.5 billion loan is included.

Biography

Born in South Africa to an engineer father and nutritionist mother, Musk left home as a 17-year-old for college in Canada, in part to avoid serving in the apartheid-era South African army.
After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania with degrees in physics and economics, he enrolled at Stanford University.
He dropped out after his first few days to pursue his three main areas of interest: the Internet, clean energy and space.
He created an online publishing platform called Zip2 in 1995 and sold it four years later for more than $300 million.
He reinvested some of the proceeds to start X.com, an online payment system.
He would merge that with what eventually became PayPal, the e-commerce site that was ultimately sold to eBay for $1.5 billion in 2002.
His next project: SpaceX, a closely held rocket company that was tapped by NASA to take over space shuttle’s role of resupplying the International Space Station.
A year later, he co-founded Tesla, the company that produced the world’s first all-electric, zero-emission sports car in 2010.
In the same year the company sold shares in a public offering.
His third company, SolarCity, was a provider of solar power systems.
SolarCity sold shares in a public offering in 2012 and was bought by Tesla on Nov.
21, 2016.
Musk, who has said he intends to retire on planet Mars, joined Warren Buffett’s Giving Pledge in April 2012.
Tesla became the world’s most valuable carmaker in July 2020 and further gains led to Musk becoming the world’s richest person in January 2021.
He announced in October 2021 that Tesla would move its headquarters from Palo Alto, California to Austin, Texas.
In April 2022 Musk made an offer to buy Twitter Inc for $44 billion after acquiring a stake in the social-media firm.
After its board agreed to recommend the deal, Musk spent months trying to terminate it.
Musk eventually purchased Twitter in October 2022.
He renamed the company X Corp.
in April 2023.

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.
The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.
Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.
The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.
Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.
The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured.
The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.
A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.
Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco.

Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces had taken control of Bab Al-Mandab and Mayun Island after clearing the area, AlArabiya reported on Friday, citing military sources.

Yemen's Houthis said Saudi strikes on a petrol station and a market killed more than a dozen people, while the Iran-backed group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding several civilians.
The Houthis last month launched a lightning offensive in Yemen, reigniting a long frozen civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government there.
They have also launched sustained attacks on Saudi Arabia itself, the world's biggest crude exporter, rattling global markets already volatile from the wider Middle East war.
Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 15 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll", in attacks it blamed on Saudi Arabia in the northwestern Jawf province, where it reported strikes on a market and a petrol station.
In Aden, two ballistic missiles struck the perimeter of the airport, leaving several civilians wounded and causing damage, government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili said on X.
He blamed the Houthis for the attack, describing it as "the sixth such attack on the airport".
A local police source told AFP that one missile fell inside the airport perimeter shortly before the Houthis issued a warning for people to evacuate the area.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden airport to immediately evacuate due to the presence of a military cargo plane belonging to the Saudi enemy transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram.
The first strike happened while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward", the first police source said.
The second attack targeted an area "under Saudi forces' control inside the perimeter of Aden airport", the second Aden police official said.
Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
Repeated Aden attacks
The Houthis have targeted Aden several times in recent weeks.
They have also intensified attacks on their Saudi foe, while they battle the government it backs in Aden, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
On Saturday, a police source told AFP that the Houthis targeted a Saudi coalition military position near the Aden airport.
It was also targeted the previous week.
Two missiles also landed within the airport perimeter earlier this month, a day after a deadly missile attack struck the presidential palace in Aden.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.

Ether fell to $2,282.46 on Binance on Saturday afternoon, its lowest since at least September, before recovering to about $2,350.
US spot ether ETFs lost about $220.7 million last week while bitcoin funds took in $301.2 million, according to Farside data.
On Thursday Ethereum's developers also pulled the Glamsterdam upgrade from its October 26 testnet date after a security firm flagged a gas-pricing risk.
The second-largest cryptocurrency has spent October doing worse than the largest.
Ether was at about $2,726 on October 5 and closed Friday, October 23, at $2,387.60, a fall of about 12%, while bitcoin lost about 6% over the same period.
On Saturday the gap widened again.
Between 14:00 and 15:15 UTC ether fell 3.6% on Binance, from $2,368 to $2,282.46, its lowest price since at least the start of September, on $139.5 million of volume in the 15:00 hour, about 21 times the hour before; bitcoin fell 1.2% to $79,220 in the same half-hour.
No single item of news was reported as the cause.
By midnight ether had recovered to $2,358.82, and on Sunday morning it traded near $2,350.
The fund flows explain more of the month than the weekend does.

ChainSecurity said it had not shown that any major live protocol was exploitable, and no new Hoodi date was set.
A revised schedule was expected after Devcon in early November.
None of this touches ether holders directly.
Mainnet had no Glamsterdam date to delay, and the change matters mainly to node operators, who had to install client releases that drop the October 26 activation.
Its market effect is about timing: an upgrade that some had hoped would reach mainnet before the end of the year now has no testnet date, let alone a mainnet one, in a month when the asset was already short of buyers.

The Federal Reserve decides on Wednesday, with futures pricing a hold and a likely December increase; Coinbase and Strategy report on Thursday after the close; and the monthly crypto options expiry falls on Friday, October 30.
Saturday's low at $2,282 was retested at $2,294.84 and held.

US spot XRP ETFs see $4.25 million in weekly inflows after brief outflow
Photo: Rafael Minguet Delgado / Pexels
XRP funds bounced back from a $1.84 million outflow week even as Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana ETFs bled capital
US spot XRP ETFs pulled in approximately $4.25 million in net inflows last week.
That reverses a $1.84 million outflow the week before, which had snapped a 13-week winning streak.
The amount is small by Wall Street standards.
The timing is more interesting: XRP products were collecting money while their Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana counterparts were losing it.
Where the money went
The rebound covered the week ending October 22-23.
Most of the action landed in just two sessions.
On October 21, the funds took in $709,000.
The next day, October 22, inflows jumped to $3.55 million, the strongest daily figure of the stretch.
Franklin Templeton’s XRPZ fund did much of the heavy lifting.
It accounted for a significant share of the week’s inflows, making it the clear driver of the recovery.
Bitwise’s XRP ETF told a messier story.
The fund logged both inflows and outflows during the week, and the result was essentially neutral activity.
The bigger scorecard
Zoom out, and the XRP ETF category has built a meaningful base since launching in November 2025.
Cumulative net inflows across the various products have reached around $1.8 billion.
Total net assets sit somewhere between $1.48 billion and $1.57 billion, depending on the reporting date.
The gap between cumulative inflows and current assets says something about the underlying token’s price.

Put plainly, investors have put more money into these funds than the funds are currently worth.
When the asset inside an ETF falls, the holdings shrink even if nobody sells a single share.
That matches what XRP itself has been doing.
The token traded in a range of $1.27 to $1.36 during the period, with resistance hovering around the $1.40 mark.
The 13-week inflow streak that ended the prior week also provides useful context.
A single $1.84 million outflow after more than three months of steady buying looked less like a stampede and more like a pause.
The following week’s $4.25 million return more than covered that loss.
Swimming against the current
The most notable part of the week is what happened elsewhere.
Spot ETFs tied to Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana all reported net outflows over the same stretch.
Solana products in particular extended an ongoing run of withdrawals.
That marks a prolonged stretch of negative sentiment toward that asset among ETF buyers.
So XRP funds were collecting money while the rest of the crypto ETF neighborhood was emptying out.
What this means
For investors, the inflow rebound signals that demand for XRP exposure through regulated wrappers has not dried up.
The concentration in Franklin Templeton’s XRPZ could point to a targeted strategy from institutional players, rather than a broad retail wave.
The disconnect between fund flows and price is the key thing to watch.

Release Date: October 6, 2026 | Forecast Completed: October 1, 2026 | Next Release Date: November 10, 2026
We forecast the Brent crude oil spot price will average $105/b in the fourth quarter of 2026 (4Q26), $14/b higher than in last month’s STEO.
We assess that crude oil production shut-ins averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from 5.8 million b/d in August and down from 10.9 million b/d at the peak in May.

 most notable among these developments were attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, which temporarily halted flows on a crucial bypass used to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the attacks, we estimate this pipeline was shipping more than 5.0 million barrels per day (b/d) of oil exports via Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port on the Red Sea.
The disruption of the pipeline led to the daily Brent spot price reaching as high as $131/b on September 15, as buyers scrambled to secure near-term supplies due to the loss of Saudi exports.
Daily prices eased somewhat during the last week of September as the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia was repaired and partially resumed flows as of September 22.
Some of the decrease in Red Sea exports has been offset by shifting exports back through the Strait of Hormuz.
Ship tracking data from Vortexa indicates that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz increased slightly in September as Saudi Arabia increasingly used ship-to-ship transfers along Oman’s coast.
We estimate that oil exports from the Middle East increased in September compared with August despite the increase in attacks, and we estimate that crude oil production shut-ins fell.
We assess that crude oil production shut-ins averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from 5.8 million b/d in August and down from 10.9 million b/d at the peak in May.
We forecast the Brent crude oil spot price will average $105/b in the fourth quarter of 2026 (4Q26), $14/b higher than in last month’s STEO.
We assume that oil flows from the Middle East remain constrained through 4Q26, leading to shut-in production averaging 4.5 million b/d during that quarter.
With export routes still constrained, the attacks on the East-West pipeline highlight the potential for continued volatility in physical oil flows and oil prices amid ongoing withdrawals from oil inventories.
The heightened risk associated with oil tankers transiting the region has added to shipping costs and increased the risk premium reflected in oil prices.
High tanker rates, which reached record levels in September, reflect increasing insurance costs and are putting additional upward pressure on delivered crude oil prices to refiners.
Ships are also taking longer routes to avoid conflict zones, which is limiting the number of available vessels.

No candidate in either race won a majority (50%+) as required by Georgia State law, forcing run-off elections for both seats held on January 5, 2021.
Senator Perdue's term expired on January 3, 2021, resulting in a vacancy until the winner of the run-off election was sworn in.
Democrats Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock defeated Perdue and Loeffler, respectively, in the run-off elections and were sworn in on January 20, bringing the party division to 50 Republicans, 48 Democrats, and 2 Independents (who caucus with the Democrats).
Democrats hold the majority due to the tie-breaking vote of Vice President Kamala Harris.

The most vulnerable senators of 2026 less than a week before Election Day
Republican incumbents occupy first seven spots on final list of the cycle
When CQ Roll Call first published this list for the 2026 election cycle a year and a half ago, Georgia Sen.
Jon Ossoff was ranked the most vulnerable incumbent senator.
Things have changed.
Just under a week out from Election Day, Ossoff now sits at the tail end of the rankings.
Inside Elections with Nathan L.
Gonzales rates his reelection race as Lean Democratic, and major outside groups from both parties have pulled their ad spending from the state in recent weeks.
Ossoff’s drop is among a few changes we’ve made as we revisit this list for the final time before the midterm elections.
The Senate battleground has remained relatively stable since the end of last month, with control of the chamber on the line.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win the majority — a prospect that looked highly unlikely for much of the cycle.
The top four most vulnerable incumbent senators — Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Roger Marshall of Kansas — are the same as our list from a month ago.
While Husted, Collins and Sullivan have been in competitive races all year, Democrats continue to see deep-red Kansas as a pickup opportunity, and Inside Elections shifted the race rating in Democrats’ direction earlier this month.
Other incumbents on this list, such as South Carolina’s Darline Graham and new entrant Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, face tougher-than-expected paths to reelection but remain favored to hold their seats.
Still, their inclusion illustrates the tough environment Republicans find themselves in as they defend seats in deep-red territory that weren’t expected to be part of the battleground two years ago.
Nebraska’s Pete Ricketts remains on the list but falls a spot to No.
7 as the Republican appears to be in a stronger position to defeat independent Dan Osborn.
Races for a half-dozen open seats, which are not included on this list of vulnerable incumbents, will also be crucial to determining Senate control.
Republicans have pickup opportunities in Michigan, Minnesota and Ne
[...]
and also win over a certain chunk of Republican voters.
After narrowly losing to Republican Deb Fischer two years ago, independent Dan Osborn is now challenging Ricketts, a former two-term governor and one of the wealthiest members of Congress.
Osborn, a former union leader, has leaned into economic populism, casting Ricketts as an out-of-touch nepo baby.
After Republicans circulated leaked audio of Osborn disparaging rural Trump voters, the independent candidate apologized.
Despite Ricketts’ personal wealth, he’s getting an outside boost from the crypto-related Defend American Jobs super PAC.
While there’s no Democrat on the ballot, Osborn could be hurt by the presence of three third-party candidates, though one has since dropped out and endorsed him.
Since topping our initial list of the most vulnerable senators, Ossoff has seen nearly everything go right for him.
He raised an eye-popping $136.6 million through Oct.
14, swamping his Republican rival, Rep.
Mike Collins, who brought in $10.7 million.
Polls show him consistently in the lead.
Collins has been dogged by a House Ethics inquiry and reports that his son-in-law shared antisemitic and white nationalist social media posts.
At this point, the GOP’s main hope is that Ossoff somehow gets less than 50 percent, forcing him into a Dec.
1 runoff that could draw big spending if Senate control is on the line.
Ryan Kelly contributed to this report.

Live Rischio 5/5
Termina tra
Come partecipare
- Leggere la clausola 1.8 dei termini: la Francia e altri 11 paesi UE sono esclusi, l'Italia non è nominata e l'elenco non è esaustivo.
- Aprire https://1wtoken.com/ digitando l'indirizzo; non è stato ancora pubblicato alcun indirizzo di mint del token.
- La pagina richiede un wallet Solana non custodial; nessun account né KYC.
- I versamenti sono in USDC su Solana (minimo 10 USDC) e non si possono annullare.
- Il conto alla rovescia termina il 30 ottobre 2026 alle 16:00 UTC; l'assegnazione è proporzionale dopo la chiusura.
- Token e USDC non utilizzati tornano al wallet; la società non ha indicato date per nessuno dei due.
La nostra analisi
La vendita di token 1win è aperta su Solana.
1win, marchio di casinò online e scommesse sportive, offre al pubblico 130 milioni di token dalla propria pagina di vendita, a prezzo fisso di 0,03 USDC ciascuno.
Quando abbiamo letto la pagina, alle 07:20 UTC del 17 ottobre 2026, 1.885 wallet avevano versato 5.660.925 dollari a fronte di un obiettivo di 3,9 milioni, cioè 1,45 volte quanto serve alla vendita.
Ogni token acquistato nella vendita si sblocca per intero alla generazione del token (TGE, token generation event).
Questo è un articolo di cronaca e verifica, non un invito a partecipare.
Per chi legge dall’Italia il punto è questo: l’Italia non compare nell’elenco dei paesi esclusi dai termini, ma l’elenco è introdotto da «inclusi, ma non limitati a» e le clausole di chiusura valgono comunque.
Non esiste un white paper MiCA che abbiamo potuto trovare, non c’è alcun controllo KYC e i termini non nominano mai la società che emette il token.
La Francia, invece, è esclusa per nome insieme a undici altri paesi dell’Unione europea.
Il token ha poi due nomi.
Il LitePaper, l’account X del progetto e i comunicati lo chiamano 1win Token ($1WIN).
La pagina di vendita e i termini lo chiamano 1w Token (1W).
Chi è escluso dalla vendita di token 1win
La clausola 1.8 dei termini e condizioni (aggiornati al 5 ottobre 2026) vieta la partecipazione a residenti e cittadini di 31 paesi indicati per nom
[...]
icabile e tribunali sono quelli «stabiliti dalla Società» (12.1).
La clausola 1.1 definisce questa Società con le sole parole «1w Token»: nessuna ragione sociale, nessun indirizzo, nessun numero di registrazione.
Né il sito, né il LitePaper, né i termini citano MiCA, antiriciclaggio o KYC.
Il LitePaper è un documento di marketing, non un white paper MiCA; la nostra guida al MiCA spiega che cosa deve pubblicare un’offerta di token conforme alle norme europee.
Come funzionano il pool e i rimborsi
L’assegnazione segue un pool a sottoscrizione eccedente, non il criterio «chi arriva prima».
Chi partecipa collega un wallet Solana non custodial (non si crea alcun account) e versa USDC su Solana, da 10 USDC e senza massimo.
Dopo la chiusura, ogni wallet riceve una quota dei 130 milioni di token pari alla sua quota sull’intero pool.
Viene trattenuto solo l’importo in USDC necessario a pagare quella quota; il resto va restituito al wallet (clausola 3.3.5).
Se la vendita non avesse raggiunto l’obiettivo, i token invenduti sarebbero stati bruciati.

That is about 1.57 times the 130,000,000 tokens on offer at $0.03, an allocation worth $3.9 million.

How do you feel about ETH today?
About Ethereum
Ethereum is a blockchain platform that enables developers to build and deploy smart contracts and decentralized applications, operating through thousands of independent nodes worldwide rather than through a central authority.
-
Smart Contract Pioneer: Ethereum introduced programmable smart contracts that automatically execute agreements when predetermined conditions are met, revolutionizing how digital transactions and applications function.
-
Proof of Stake Security: Following The Merge in September 2022, Ethereum transitioned from energy-intensive mining to an efficient Proof of Stake consensus mechanism, reducing energy consumption by over 99%.
-
Programmable Money: Ether (ETH) serves as both the native currency for transactions and the fuel that powers decentralized finance applications, NFT marketplaces, and thousands of decentralized applications across its ecosystem.
What Is the Difference Between Ethereum and Ether (ETH)?
-
Ethereum is the network.
It is the decentralized, global blockchain platform that runs smart contracts and supports applications.
Think of it as a global computer or an operating system.
-
Ether (ETH) is the cryptocurrency.
It is the native token or "fuel" of the Ethereum network.
ETH is used to pay transaction fees (known as "gas") and to secure the network through staking.
Ether is the asset that is bought, sold, and traded on exchanges.
How Does Ethereum Work?
Ethereum operates as a global, decentralized computer that executes programs called smart contracts.
The network consists of thousands of independent nodes operated by individuals and organizations worldwide, all maintaining a shared record of transactions and data.
When someone initiates a transaction or interacts with an application on Ethereum, validators process and confirm these actions, adding them to the blockchain permanently.
Unlike traditional centralized systems where a single entity controls operations, Ethereum distributes authority across its entire network.
This design ensures that no single party can manipulate transactions or shut down applications.
The network's native cryptocurrency, ether, serves multiple purposes: it pays for transaction fees, compensates validators for securing the network, and functions as collateral in various financial applications.
Smart Contracts & EVM
Smart contracts are self-executing programs stored on the Ethereum blockchain that automatically carry out agreements when specific conditions are met.
Written primarily in Solidity, a programming language designed for Ethereum, these contracts run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine, which acts as a global computing platform distributed across thousands of nodes.
The EVM ensures that smart contracts execute identically on every computer in the network, creating a trustworthy environment where outcomes are predictable and tamper-proof.
Developers can build anything from simple payment systems to complex financial instruments, gaming platforms, and decentralized organizations.
Once deployed, smart contracts operate autonomously without the need for intermediaries, and their code remains publicly verifiable on the blockchain.
This programmability distinguishes Ethereum from Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies focused solely on transferring value.
Applications built on Ethereum can hold and transfer assets, enforce rules, manage identities, and coordinate activities between multiple parties without traditional intermediaries like banks, brokers, or administrators.
Proof of Stake
Ethereum secures its network through Proof of Stake, a consensus mechanism that replaced the previous Proof of Work system in September 2022.
Under Proof of Stake, validators stake their ether (ETH) as collateral to participate in proposing and validating new blocks of transactions.
The network randomly selects validators to create blocks and confirm transactions based on their staked amount and other factors.
Validators earn rewards for honestly performing their duties but face penalties, known as slashing, if they act maliciously or fail to maintain their nodes properly.
This economic incentive structure ensures network security without requiring massive computational power.
A validator who attempts to approve fraudulent transactions or goes offline repeatedly risks losing a portion of their staked ether.
The transition to Proof of Stake brought multiple benefits.
Energy consumption dropped by approximately 99.95%, making Ethereum environmentally sustainable.
The mechanism also strengthened decentralization by lowering barriers to participation compared to the mining equipment required under Proof of Work.
Additionally, Proof of Stake established the foundation for future scalability improvements through technologies like danksharding.
How to Stake ETH
ETH holders can help secure the network and earn rewards by staking their ether.
Annual yields typically vary, often ranging between 3-5%.
Participants can choose different methods based on their technical skill and the amount of ETH they have.
Options range from running a dedicated 'solo' validator (which requires 32 ETH) , using a "staking as a service" provider , joining a pooled staking platform with a smaller amount, or using the staking services offered by centralized exchanges.
What Makes Ethereum Unique?
-
Programmable Platform: Unlike Bitcoin, which functions primarily as a digital currency, Ethereum operates as a global application platform where developers can create any type of decentralized service through smart contracts
-
Largest DeFi Ecosystem: The network hosts over $14 billion locked in DeFi applications, with hundreds of thousands of active users interacting with financial protocols, NFT marketplaces, gaming platforms, and social applications daily
-
True Decentralization: Thousands of independent validators operate globally with no central authority controlling development or operations, ensuring applications continue functioning regardless of jurisdictional restrictions
-
Developer Network Effect: The largest community of blockchain developers builds on Ethereum, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where more developers attract more users and applications
History of Ethereum
Vitalik Buterin proposed Ethereum in late 2013 as a blockchain platform that could support applications beyond simple currency transfers.
Buterin envisioned a network where developers could build decentralized versions of traditional services using smart contracts.
Following a crowdfunding campaign in mid-2014 that raised over $18 million, Ethereum launched its mainnet in July 2015.
The network gained attention in 2017 when Initial Coin Offerings built on Ethereum raised billions of dollars for blockchain projects.

Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly 48% to 46% in a new St.
Pete Polls survey of the Governor’s race for Florida Politics.
It is the first time in three surveys by the pollster that either candidate has led by more than a tenth of a point.
The sample assumes an electorate 12 points more Republican than Democratic.
Ballots cast through Tuesday morning are less than a point apart.
Another 3% picked someone else and 3% are undecided.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2 percentage points, and Donalds’ lead is inside it.
Republicans hold a registration advantage of roughly 1.5 million voters over Democrats, nearly 5.69 million to almost 4.15 million at the Oct.
5 book closing, with another 3.35 million registered to no party.
That is R+8 on the rolls.
The poll’s sample is R+12.
St.
Pete Polls’ mid-September survey had Donalds at 44% and Jolly at 43%, a tenth of a point apart before rounding.
Its Oct.
5-7 survey had them tied at 45%, again a tenth of a point apart.
Undecided voters have gone from 9% to 7% to 3% across the three polls.
Donalds is up 3 points since the October survey and Jolly is up 1.
That movement sits inside the margin of error of either poll.
Forty-six percent of respondents said they had already voted.
Jolly leads that group 58% to 38%.
Donalds leads the 54% who still plan to vote 57% to 34%.
In the unweighted sample, 55% of Democrats said they had already voted.
Among Republicans, 39% had.
As of Tuesday morning, 1,257,198 Republicans and 1,244,432 Democrats had cast ballots by mail or at early voting sites, per the Division of Elections.
That is a Republican edge of 12,766 votes out of 3.15 million cast, four-tenths of a point.
Democrats lead the mail vote 643,143 to 529,943.
Republicans lead in-person early voting 727,255 to 601,289.
At the same point in 2022, Republicans led Democrats in ballots cast by about 177,000.
Reweighted to an R+10 electorate, the same responses produce a 47% to 46% race.
At R+9 it is a tie, and at the registration split Jolly is ahead by a point.
Jolly leads independents 56% to 34%, up from 49% to 33% in the October survey.
Donalds holds 81% of Republicans and Jolly holds 81% of Democrats.
Each takes about 14% of the other party.
Voters 70 and older back Donalds 65% to 31%.
Jolly leads every younger group: 60% to 30% among voters under 30, 54% to 37% among those 30 to 49, and 49% to 45% among those 50 to 69.
Donalds leads the Tampa market 52% to 43% and Fort Myers 62% to 35%.
Miami and West Palm Beach are tied at 47% apiece, and Orlando is within a point.
The University of North Florida’s survey released last week had Donalds ahead 49% to 47%.
St.
Pete Polls surveyed 916 likely voters Oct.
25-27 for Florida Politics, using automated phone calls for 71% of responses and peer-to-peer text messages for 29%.
Respondents were drawn at random from the state’s registered voter file as of Oct.
14.
Results were weighted by political party, race, age, gender, and media market to match Florida’s active voter population.
The weighted sample is 43% Republican, 31% Democratic, and 27% other.
Voters who said they do not plan to vote in the General Election were excluded.

The 2026 United States Senate election in Minnesota will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the state of Minnesota.
Democratic lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan and Republican former journalist Michele Tafoya are the nominees for their respective parties.
Democratic incumbent Tina Smith is not seeking a second full term.[1]
After Smith announced she would not run for reelection, Flanagan and congresswoman Angie Craig sought the Democratic nomination, which Flanagan won on August 11 with 59% of the vote.
Tafoya won the Republican nomination with 52.1% of the vote over Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze and former basketball player Royce White.
This will be the first Senate election in Minnesota without an incumbent since 2006.[2] Republicans have not won a Senate election in Minnesota since 2002.

My decision, then, has nothing to do with politics.
It’s entirely personal.

WASHINGTON, DC – Today, U.S.
Senator Tina Smith (D-MN), penned an op-ed in the Minnesota Star Tribune announcing her decision not to seek re-election to the United States Senate once her six-year term ends in 2027.
During her tenure, Senator Smith has lowered costs for prescription drugs, fought for true mental health parity, helped to pass the most significant climate legislation in history, and served as a champion for rural communities.
She plans to carry forward her work standing up for all Minnesotans in the Senate – whether it is protecting access to reproductive care, lowering housing costs, defending the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, or getting a new Farm Bill across the finish line.
A full list of Senator Smith’s accomplishments is available here.
You can read Senator Smith’s op-ed explaining her decision here and below.
Additionally, Senator Smith spoke about her decision in a video address to Minnesota, that you can watch here:
Dear Minnesota
Sen.
Tina Smith
I wanted you to hear directly from me that I have decided not to run for re-election to the U.S.
Senate in 2026.
I know my decision may come as a surprise.
After all, we live in a time when elected officials tend to continue their service well past what the rest of us consider to be “retirement age.” And I understand, I really do, why it’s so hard for people to walk away from this job.
I’ll never have a greater honor than working for the people of Minnesota.
That said, politicians are human beings.
As much as I love my work, I’m fortunate enough to be able to say that my work is only part of what makes up my life.
And after two decades of hard, rewarding work in public service, I’m ready to prioritize other things—starting with my family.
Time flies.
When I got to the Senate, Archie and I weren’t grandparents, but now we have four grandkids, all under the age of five.
And with our sons Sam and Mason and our daughters-in-law Emily and Julia all living in Minnesota for the first time, we plan to spend lots of time with them, as well as with my dad, who turns 95 this June, and our entire extended family of siblings, nieces, and nephews.
Archie and I have been married for 41 years, and we have a lot we’re looking forward to doing together, but a big part of the plan involves simply being around to cook dinners, organize sleepovers, go on field trips, and just step in whenever an extra pair of hands are needed.
My decision, then, has nothing to do with politics.
It’s entirely personal.
But it’s not lost on me that I’m stepping away from elected office at a time when strong, progressive leadership in Washington is more important than ever.
As much as I’m looking forward to whatever new adventure awaits in this big, complicated, beautiful world, I know I will be leaving Minnesota’s next Senator with some critical work to do.
I’m keeping in mind two things.

The 2026 United States Senate election in New Hampshire will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the state of New Hampshire.
Democratic congressman Chris Pappas and Republican former senator John Sununu are the nominees for their respective parties.
Democratic incumbent Jeanne Shaheen is not seeking re-election to a fourth term.
Primary elections were held on September 8.
Pappas won the Democratic nomination with 65% of the vote against medical scientist Karishma Manzur.
Sununu won the Republican primary nomination with 68.5% of the vote against former Massachusetts senator Scott Brown.
This will be the first open Senate election in New Hampshire since 2010.
Republicans have not won a Senate election in New Hampshire since that race.
Background
[edit]
New Hampshire is considered a slightly to moderately blue state at the federal level, with Kamala Harris carrying the state by roughly 3 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
The state's congressional delegation has been entirely Democratic since 2017.
However, Republicans control the governorship, both state legislative chambers, and a majority in the executive council.[1][2]
Shaheen was first elected in 2008, defeating incumbent John Sununu in a rematch of 2002, and was reelected in 2014 and 2020.[3] Republicans have not won a U.S.
Senate race in New Hampshire since 2010.[4]

found an electorate where Trump is so unpopular ...
that voters appeared more inclined to cast their ballots based on the Senate candidates’ party affiliations in an election they view as a referendum on Trump’s presidency." According to reporting from AP, "Steve Marchand, a Democratic consultant and former New Hampshire gubernatorial candidate, said Sununu has benefited from national money that got redirected from other states that are no longer seen as top targets, while Democrats were slower to invest."
