Only 38% of respondents approve of Trump’s job performance, while 62% disapprove.
Governor Kelly Ayotte leads Cinde Warmington 50%-42%, with 51% approving of Ayotte’s job performance.

The October poll from the Saint Anselm College Survey Center (SACSC) at the New Hampshire Institute of Politics (NHIOP) finds Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot 52%-43%, as economic concerns and President Donald Trump’s unpopularity shape the political environment ahead of the elections.
Only 38% of respondents approve of Trump’s job performance, while 62% disapprove.
Economy and inflation rank as voters’ top concerns at 19%, followed by elections and democracy at 18% and affordability at 17%.
Democratic voters also report greater enthusiasm for voting, with 98% saying they are extremely likely to vote, compared with 92% of Republicans.
In the U.S.
Senate race, Democrat Chris Pappas leads former Senator John E.
Sununu 50%-43%, although both have net-negative favorability ratings.
Pappas is viewed favorably by 41% of respondents and unfavorably by 56%, while Sununu’s ratings stand at 40% favorable and 56% unfavorable, reflecting the broader challenges facing both candidates.
In the more competitive 1st Congressional District, Democrat Stefany Shaheen trails the generic Democratic ballot benchmark but leads Republican Anthony DiLorenzo by 4 points (46%-42%).
As in the Senate race, both candidates have net-negative favorability, though the political environment favors the Democrat.
In the more Democratic-leaning 2nd Congressional District, Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander faces limited negative campaigning and maintains a favorable image along with a 16-point lead, 54%-38%.
She is one of only two major-office candidates with a net-positive image (49%-42%), while Republican Lily Tang Williams is slightly net-negative (35%-37%).
Governor Kelly Ayotte leads Cinde Warmington 50%-42%, with 51% approving of Ayotte’s job performance.
The property tax cap referendum receives 57% support, short of the 60% threshold required for passage in individual localities.
In the potential 2028 presidential primaries, Pete Buttigieg leads the Democratic field with 28%, followed by Jon Ossoff at 14%.
On the Republican side, Vice President J.D.
Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are tied at 38%.
New Hampshire Institute of Politics Executive Director Neil Levesque summarized the results: “The upcoming election is taking shape in a political environment where inflation and affordability remain central concerns, presenting challenges for the party in power.
Public views of many candidates for top offices are mixed, while Democratic voters appear somewhat more energized, in part reflecting their views of President Donald Trump and his administration.
These dynamics, alongside ongoing economic concerns, are likely to shape the electoral landscape.”
These results are from a Saint Anselm College Survey Center poll based on online surveys of 1672 New Hampshire likely voters.

LOWELL, Mass.
– Less than a week before the general election, voters in New Hampshire are narrowly divided on whom they’ll support in races for U.S.
Senate and governor, while voters in Massachusetts appear more decisive, with the exception of ballot questions calling for all-party primaries and looser restrictions on single-family housing.
Voters in New Hampshire and Massachusetts responded to two separate UMass Lowell/YouGov surveys, results of which were released Wednesday.
Early voting is already underway ahead of the Nov.
3 election.
New Hampshire: Pappas, Ayotte slightly ahead in respective races
In the Granite State race for U.S.
Senate, the survey of 600 likely voters shows Democratic U.S.
Rep.
Chris Pappas is slightly ahead of Republican former U.S.
Sen.
John E.
Sununu, 48% to 41%, while 4% of respondents support Constitution Party candidate Edmond LaPlante and 7% are undecided.
“While the Democrats are polling well nationally in the 2026 midterms, their pathway to control of the Senate is extremely narrow.
New Hampshire is a state they cannot lose.
Pappas is holding the line against Sununu, but this race, like most statewide races in New Hampshire in recent memory, remains close,” said UMass Lowell Professor Joshua Dyck, co-director of the university’s Center for Public Opinion and chair of the Political Science Department.
In the governor’s race, poll results show incumbent Republican Gov.
Kelly Ayotte slightly ahead of Democratic former executive councilor Cinde Warmington, 48% to 42%, while 3% of respondents support Libertarian candidate Stephen Villee and 7% are undecided.
“From 2016 on, Democrats have consistently won Senate races in New Hampshire, while Republicans have consistently won governor’s races, and this year appears no different.
New Hampshire appears to have the most consistent ticket-splitting behavior pattern in the country,” said John Cluverius, the center’s co-director and an associate professor of political science.
Fielded from Oct.
2 through Oct.
19, the New Hampshire poll carries an adjusted margin of error of +/- 5 percentage points.
Massachusetts: Markey, Healey in the driver’s seat
Incumbent Democratic Gov.
Maura Healey also holds a commanding lead.
She is 28 percentage points ahead of Republican challenger Mike Minogue in the governor’s race, according to the survey, with 57% support from respondents, compared with Minogue’s 29%.
Independent candidate and activist Andrea James trails with 4%, while 8% are undecided and 2% said they will not vote.
“Massachusetts was already deep blue in presidential elections, but these poll results show an even worse environment for Republicans this year.
Less than 80% of Trump voters plan to vote for the Republican nominee for governor, and less than 70% of respondents who voted for Trump in 2024 say they’ll vote for the Republican nominee for U.S.
Senate.
Massachusetts Republicans haven’t found the bottom yet,” Cluverius said.
Fielded from Oct.
7 through Oct.
18, the Massachusetts survey of 850 likely voters carries a margin of error of +/- 4.4 percentage points.
Presidential approval ratings a liability for Republicans
Trump receives low marks as president from a majority of respondents in both polls.
Among likely Granite State likely voters, 61% disapprove of his job performance.
Notably, 22% of self-identified Republicans and 24% of respondents who said they voted for Trump in 2024 disapprove of the job he is doing.
In the Bay State poll, 74% of respondents disapprove of Trump’s job performance, while 25% approve, resulting in a -49 net approval, lower than the -36 net approval recorded in a 2020 UMass Lowell/YouGov poll of Massachusetts registered voters.
Polls: AI does not always compute
Survey respondents in both states also find common ground when it comes to AI data centers.
In the New Hampshire poll, more than two-thirds of respondents (67%) oppose the construction of an AI data center in their community, including 44% who voted for Trump in 2024.
Further, 62% support a statewide ban on data center construction and expansion.
The results are much the same in Massachusetts where 72% of poll respondents oppose the construction of an AI data center in their community, including 44% of respondents who voted for Donald Trump in 2024.
Fifty-two percent support a statewide ban on data center construction and expansion.
